title: Mokusen's Hand
text:
Mokusen Hiki was a Zen teacher who lived in a temple in the province of Tamba. One of his followers came to him with a complaint about his wife: she was terribly stingy. She hoarded everything and would not spend or give anything away.

Mokusen went to visit the woman. When she came in, he held up his fist in front of her face, clenched tight.

"What do you mean by that?" she asked, surprised.

"Suppose my hand were always like this," he said. "What would you call it?"

"Deformed," she answered.

Then he opened his hand flat and held it out in front of her. "Suppose it were always like this. What then?"

"Another kind of deformity," she said.

"If you understand that much," said Mokusen, "you are a good wife." Then he left.

After his visit, the story says, the woman helped her husband to give as well as to save.
lesson: A household needs both saving and giving. Either one practiced all the time, with no room for the other, becomes a kind of deformity.
people: Mokusen Hiki, a disciple, the disciple's wife
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919), Mokusen's Hand
